title: null, undefined, void, and never
hook: JavaScript has two "empty" values — `null` and `undefined`. TypeScript models them as distinct types, plus `void` for functions that return nothing useful and `never` for code paths that cannot happen.

sections.heading: What are null, undefined, void, and never?

blocks.text: **`null`** means "intentionally no value." **`undefined`** means "not yet assigned" or "property missing." **`void`** is the return type of functions that do not return a meaningful value (they implicitly return `undefined`). **`never`** is the type of values that never occur — used for functions that always throw, infinite loops, or exhaustive switch branches. With `strictNullChecks` enabled (recommended), `null` and `undefined` are only assignable where explicitly allowed.

entries.plainDefinition: A value representing deliberate emptiness. In strict mode, not assignable to `string`, `number`, etc. without a union.
The default for unassigned variables, missing object properties, and functions with no return statement.
Return type for functions whose result you ignore. At run time the value is `undefined`.
The bottom type — no value satisfies it. Used for unreachable code and exhaustive checks.
entries.example: `function fail(msg: string): never { throw new Error(msg); }`

blocks.text: C# has a single `null` for reference types and `Nullable<T>` for value types. JavaScript/TypeScript has **two** absent values, which confuses teams migrating from C#. `strictNullChecks` forces you to handle both. `void` communicates intent at API boundaries — a logger returns `void`, not `any`. `never` powers exhaustiveness checking in discriminated unions (module 03).

blocks.title: C# comparison
blocks.body: C#: one `null`, plus `Nullable<int>` for missing numbers. TypeScript: `null` and `undefined` as separate types, often combined as `T | null | undefined` or shortened with `?.` and `??`.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Annotate nullable parameters
items.body: `function greet(name: string | null): void` — callers must pass string or null explicitly.

items.title: Optional properties use undefined
items.body: `interface Config { timeout?: number }` means `timeout` is `number | undefined`. Optional chaining `config?.timeout` handles both missing property and null.

items.title: void vs undefined return
items.body: Declare `(): void` for side-effect functions. You can still `return;` or `return undefined;` — void means "do not use the return value."

items.title: never for impossible paths
items.body: After narrowing all cases in a switch, assign the rest variable type `never` to catch missing cases at compile time.

diagram.title: null, undefined, void, never relationships
diagram.source:
flowchart TB
  subgraph absent ["Absent values"]
    NULL[null - intentional]
    UNDEF[undefined - missing]
  end
  subgraph returns ["Function returns"]
    VOID[void - ignore result]
    NEVER[never - unreachable]
  end
  VOID -->|"run time"| UNDEF
  FAIL["throw / infinite loop"] --> NEVER
  STRICT["strictNullChecks"] --> absent

snippet.label: null and undefined with strictNullChecks
snippet.explanation: Line 2: with `strictNullChecks`, `null` is not assignable to plain `string`. Line 4: explicit `| null` allows intentional absence. Line 5: optional property is `number | undefined`. Line 7: nullish coalescing `??` treats both `null` and `undefined` as missing.

snippet.label: void return type
snippet.explanation: Line 1: `void` signals the caller should ignore the return. Line 6: assigning the return to a variable gives `void` type (or `undefined` at run time). Prefer `void` over omitting the return type on public APIs.

snippet.label: never for exhaustive checks
snippet.explanation: Line 1: a closed union of string literals. Lines 4–8: if a new shape is added to the union but not to the switch, `shape` in the default branch is not assignable to `never` — compile error. This pattern catches incomplete switches during refactors.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Treating `null` and `undefined` as interchangeable without `??` or explicit unions. Using `void` as a type for variables (it is for function returns). Forgetting that JSON has `null` but not `undefined`. Returning `null` from a `void` function when the caller expects no value.

blocks.text: `strictNullChecks` is compile-time only — JSON, Redis, and DOM APIs still deliver null at run time. `void` is not the same as `undefined` as a type: `void` means "caller must not rely on return value." `never` is the bottom type — assignable to every type, but nothing assignable to it except `never` itself. Exhaustiveness with `never` is a key discriminated-union pattern (module 03). C# NRT and TS strictNullChecks are cousins — both optional historically, both on by default in modern templates.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying strictNullChecks prevents null at run time. Claiming void and undefined are identical types. Not knowing the difference between null (intentional) and undefined (missing).

interviewTakeaways: null is intentional absence; undefined is missing/unassigned — two distinct types.
void is for function returns you ignore; at run time it is undefined.
never is the bottom type — used for exhaustiveness and unreachable code.
60s: strictNullChecks makes null/undefined explicit in unions. void for side effects. never for impossible paths and exhaustive switches.
Follow-up: how does strictNullChecks compare to C# nullable reference types?
commonPitfalls: Treating null and undefined as the same without documenting which your API uses.
Believing strictNullChecks removes null at run time.
Strong answer: 'Two absent values in JS. strictNullChecks is compile-time. Validate at JSON boundaries. never for exhaustiveness.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript has both values at run time. TypeScript with strictNullChecks distinguishes them in the type system.
C# uses `int?` for missing numbers and `string?` for nullable references. TypeScript uses union types: `number | undefined`, `string | null`.
